Siemiatycze New Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Nowogród, Poland

Siemiatycze, first mentioned in the 15th century and granted town rights in 1542, developed significantly under Anna Jabłonowska in the late 18th century. Jews settled toward the end of the 16th century, though the community only formed at the end of the 17th, remaining under Tykocin's kehilla until independence in 1730; population reached 78% (3,600 of 4,634) by 1878, settling at 53% (4,303) by 1939. Germany occupied the town in July 1941, establishing a ghetto that August; liquidation between September-November 1942 deported residents to Treblinka. This cemetery, expanded over the years to roughly 3 hectares and fenced with a concrete-and-brick wall including a red brick gate in the interwar period, held execution victims including a mass grave of 70 people. Germans repurposed matzevot for utility use during WWII; postwar theft ensured none survived in their original locations. Communist-era construction placed Polish Motorcycle Association buildings on part of the grounds in the 1970s; a 2017 excavation behind those buildings removed a 2-meter layer of earth containing human remains, and bones continued surfacing from a nearby escarpment bordering a parking lot. A 2007 memorial plaque marks the mass-grave site, surrounded by recovered town matzevot.
